title: Variability in the analysis of a single neuroimaging dataset by many teams

cost.compute_notes: 52.3 MB derived-results deposit (Zenodo 3709275) + 1.2 MB submitted-version PDF + 4.8 MB code repository + 0.8 MB supplementary files + two HTML pages. The 1 GB image deposit (Zenodo 3528329) was deliberately NOT fetched: every question asked here is answerable from the deposited derived data, and the questions that are not are listed as open. Heaviest computations: 100,000 column permutations (13 s), 20,000-permutation AUC nulls over 7 hypotheses (3 m 50 s), a logit-normal random-intercept MLE with a simulation-based recovery selftest (5 m 47 s), and a Mantel power calibration by injection (8 m across two corpora). All numpy/scipy/sklearn, no GPU.

claims.statement: NARPS's headline dispersion statistic -- 'on average across the 9 hypotheses, 20% of teams reported a result that differs from the majority' -- is a function of the nine marginal yes-rates and NOTHING else. It is identical in every world obtained by permuting each hypothesis column independently, so it cannot distinguish scattered idiosyncratic dissent from a stable minority of dissenting pipelines.
claims.scope: Verified by construction and by direct computation on the deposited 70x9 decision matrix, not argued from the text.

quantities.name: narps_headline_after_column_permutation
quantities.baseline: same statistic recomputed after independently permuting every hypothesis column

our_assessment.why: Arithmetic, not interpretation. The statistic is correct and correctly reported; the point is what it is blind to, and c2 shows that the thing it is blind to is present.

claims.statement: Reporting a significant result in NARPS is a stable TEAM TRAIT, not per-hypothesis bad luck. The variance of per-team yes-counts is 2.26 times what independence at the same column margins gives; a quarter of teams never dissent from the majority at all, twice the null rate; and the most dissenting quartile carries 57% of all dissent.
claims.scope: 70 teams x 9 hypotheses, binary decisions. The nine hypotheses are not independent -- H1/H3 and H2/H4 are the same statistical map read in two ROIs, H7/H8/H9 are all amygdala-loss -- so the test is repeated on map-disjoint subsets and survives.

claims.statement: The team trait is a PRECISION trait: how much a pipeline declares significant, not what it estimated. A team's yes-count is predicted by image-derived precision quantities (log median suprathreshold voxels, estimated smoothness) and not at all by how much its unthresholded map resembles the consensus.
claims.scope: Team level, n = 63-70 depending on which image diagnostics exist. 'Answer-side' is operationalised as NARPS's own median_pattern_corr -- the median Spearman correlation of a team's unthresholded maps with the mean pattern across teams.

quantities.name: cv_r2_yescount_from_precision_block
quantities.ci: +/- 0.024 over 25 repeats of 10-fold ridge; permuted baseline -0.046
quantities.baseline: on all 70 teams, with 6 missing-smoothness teams imputed, the same model gives -0.009: six rows of noise erase it

quantities.name: narps_own_delta_pseudo_r2_team_factors_summed
quantities.baseline: smoothness 0.0367 + software package 0.0400 + correction method 0.0237, from the deposited SuppTable4.tsv; independent estimator, same magnitude as our 0.111

our_assessment.why: Two independent estimators (our out-of-fold ridge, their in-sample mixed logistic) land on ~0.11 for the same team-level factors. The answer-side variable is flat in both.

claims.statement: The Breznau design transplanted: coded pipeline CHOICES predict the precision of the resulting image very strongly and the image itself not at all, out of fold. log(resels) R2 = +0.507; the team's correlation with the consensus map R2 = -0.073; the team's conclusion R2 = -0.103.
claims.scope: 70 teams, 39 dummy predictors built only from choices a team made (software, applied smoothing, fMRIPrep, movement modelling, correction family, statistic type, ROI-definition style, n kept) -- never a property of the image produced. 10-fold ridge, 25 repeats.

our_assessment.why: The scalar out-of-fold result reproduces the CRI shape in a third field. But c6 shows the same choices DO carry information about the map when tested pairwise, so 'not at all' here means 'not recoverable by a linear model of the level at n = 70', not 'no association'.

claims.statement: For six of seven hypotheses, how strongly two teams' unthresholded maps correlate carries no detectable information about whether they reach the same binary conclusion. Among pairs whose maps correlate above r = 0.8 on hypothesis 1 -- median r = 0.88 -- 53.4% still disagree, which is if anything worse than the marginal-implied chance rate.
claims.scope: 14,112 team-pairs over 7 hypotheses. Null permutes which team holds which decision, leaving the entire correlation matrix and the published marginal untouched; 20,000 permutations per hypothesis. Bonferroni over 7 tests is alpha = 0.0071.

quantities.name: mean_within_hypothesis_auc_mapcorr_predicts_decision_agreement
quantities.baseline: chance 0.500; per hypothesis 0.397 to 0.762

quantities.name: n_hypotheses_with_significant_mapcorr_decision_link
quantities.baseline: only H5 (AUC 0.762, p = 0.0002) survives Bonferroni; H6 p = 0.010 does not

quantities.name: disagreement_rate_among_pairs_with_map_r_above_0.8_hyp1
quantities.baseline: permutation null 45.8%, 95% interval [35.4, 52.7]

quantities.name: disagreement_rate_among_pairs_with_map_r_above_0.8_hyp5
quantities.baseline: permutation null 26.8% [13.3, 38.6] -- the one hypothesis where map similarity does predict agreement

quantities.name: excess_pairwise_agreement_over_marginal_chance
quantities.baseline: REPORTED AS A NON-FINDING: this equals the finite-population correction [k(k-1)+(n-k)(n-k-1)]/[n(n-1)] exactly and carries no information. It looked like a result and is not one.

our_assessment.why: NARPS states this qualitatively ('teams with highly correlated underlying statistical maps nonetheless reported highly divergent hypothesis outcomes'). The number and its null are new. The null is exact and conditional: it changes nothing the paper reports.

claims.statement: REFUTES THE STRONG FORM OF OUR OWN THROUGH-LINE. Pipeline choices carry real information about the ESTIMATE, not only about its precision. Team-by-team choice distance is coupled to map distance at Mantel rho = 0.193 (p = 0.0021), and 0.142 (p = 0.0117) after partialling out the smoothness channel.
claims.scope: 64 teams, 2,016 pairs. Choice distance = Gower over the coded pipeline table; map distance = 1 - Spearman r averaged over the seven deposited hypotheses; null permutes team labels. Significant on 6 of 7 hypotheses taken separately (rho 0.12-0.24).

quantities.name: mantel_choices_vs_precision
quantities.baseline: null 95th percentile 0.084; p = 0.0001

quantities.name: mantel_choices_vs_map_distance
quantities.baseline: null 95th percentile 0.106; p = 0.0021

quantities.name: partial_mantel_choices_vs_map_given_precision
quantities.baseline: null 95th percentile 0.104; p = 0.0117. Only about a quarter of the choices-map coupling runs through smoothness.

quantities.name: mantel_choices_vs_binary_conclusion
quantities.baseline: null 95th percentile 0.072; p = 0.41

our_assessment.why: This is the claim that cost me a previous conclusion, so it was attacked before it was believed: the smoothness channel is partialled out and survives; the same statistic on the conclusion returns 0.007, so the instrument is not simply positive on everything; and the machinery is validated against scipy in mantel_fast.selftest(). See c8 for a limitation that makes 0.193 a LOWER bound, not an upper one.

claims.statement: Applying one common thresholding rule to every team's unthresholded map leaves the ORDERING of the nine hypotheses nearly untouched (Spearman 0.78-0.92) and moves the LEVEL by up to 55 percentage points. The number of hypotheses on which a majority of teams find significance goes 1 -> 3 -> 4 out of 9 on identical maps.
claims.scope: NARPS's own re-thresholding, deposited as figures/ThresholdSimulation/simulation_results.csv, in two variants: uncorrected p<0.001 with k>10, and FDR, each with a common anatomical ROI. NARPS reports that the dispersion across teams is qualitatively similar; the level is not reported.

quantities.baseline: hypothesis 2: 0.214 as reported, 0.766 under common FDR. Mean absolute shift 0.160.

quantities.name: hypotheses_with_majority_significant_by_rule
quantities.value: 1 as reported / 3 at p<0.001,k>10 / 4 under FDR

our_assessment.why: Read straight off NARPS's own deposited table; the arithmetic on top of it is trivial and checkable. The framing -- ranking stable, level not -- is ours.

claims.statement: OUR OWN CRI CONCLUSION MUST BE RESTATED AS A BOUND. Applying the same pairwise instrument to the Crowdsourced Replication Initiative gives choices ~ estimate rho = 0.120 (p = 0.118) -- and injection calibration shows both designs need rho ~ 0.21-0.23 for 80% power, so CRI's number is 'cannot tell', not 'absent'. The two corpora are not shown to differ.
claims.scope: CRI at team level within each dependent variable, pooled over 6 DVs with one permutation applied to all six (48 common teams); the DVs are six different questions and pooling across them without that constraint would be wrong. Power calibrated by injecting a controlled association along the dominant axis of choice variation, 200-300 simulations per strength.

our_assessment.why: Two errors of mine are recorded here rather than tidied: a null that did not do what it was written to do, caught by measuring it instead of trusting it; and a published 'nothing' that was an undetectable-not-absent. The withdrawn number is left in the record with its retraction reason so nobody re-quotes it.

claims.statement: Analysts have almost no insight into their own analytic idiosyncrasy. Self-rated similarity to other teams is weakly calibrated to the actual similarity of their map (rho = 0.19), carries no information about whether their conclusion matches the pooled meta-analysis (rho = 0.048, p = 0.21), and is NEGATIVELY related to agreeing with the majority (rho = -0.195 excluding the one hypothesis whose majority is 'yes', p < 0.0001). Confidence behaves identically and is largely the same scale (rho = 0.670).
claims.scope: 630 team-hypothesis ratings on 1-10 scales, rank-transformed within hypothesis, p-values from permuting whole teams because a team contributes nine rows. NARPS's supplement relates both ratings to the team's own binary outcome; it does not ask whether they are calibrated against anything external.

quantities.name: spearman_confidence_vs_selfrated_similarity
quantities.ci: p < 0.0001 -- the two scales are largely one scale

quantities.name: hypotheses_where_team_majority_contradicts_image_based_meta_analysis
quantities.baseline: hypotheses 2, 4 and 6: the IBMA finds the effect, a majority of individual teams does not

our_assessment.why: The mechanism is visible per hypothesis and is not a pooling artefact: on the eight hypotheses whose majority is 'no', dissenters rate themselves MORE similar; on H5, whose majority is 'yes', dissenters rate themselves far LESS similar (5.27 vs 8.12). The rating tracks 'I found the effect', not 'I resemble my colleagues'.

claims.statement: DEFECT, verified in the published version. Extended Data Table 1's two rating columns are transposed: the column headed 'Median confidence level' is the median of the deposited `Similar` variable and the column headed 'Median similarity estimation' is the median of `Confidence`, 9 of 9 rows in both directions including the median absolute deviations. The Supplementary Information uses the same two variables correctly.

The deposited Table1.tsv emits medianSimilar before medianConfidence while the table heads them confidence-first, which is the likely origin. Consequence is small: no claim in the paper depends on these two columns.

claims.statement: Three quarters of the prediction markets' squared error is a single constant offset. A hypothesis-blind constant beats both markets on absolute error; remove the offset and the team market beats every baseline. Discrimination was excellent and calibration was absent, and reporting only the rank correlation flatters.
claims.scope: 9 hypotheses, two markets (83 and 65 active traders). Both published MAEs reproduce exactly from Supplementary Data 1. n = 9 is tiny and the paper says so; the decomposition does not need power, the comparison tests do and do not have it.

quantities.name: team_market_mae
quantities.baseline: reproduces the paper's 0.323 exactly

quantities.name: leave_one_out_constant_mae
quantities.baseline: each hypothesis predicted by the mean of the other eight; no hypothesis-specific information at all. Beats both markets. Wilcoxon vs team market p = 0.43, vs non-team p = 0.074.

quantities.name: team_market_bias_share_of_mse
quantities.baseline: bias +0.323; non-team market 78%, bias +0.414

quantities.name: team_market_debiased_rmse
quantities.baseline: from 0.375 raw; the leave-one-out constant's RMSE is 0.261, so after one constant the market is the better forecaster

quantities.name: team_market_spearman_on_five_map_disjoint_hypotheses
quantities.baseline: 0.962 over all nine (permutation p = 0.00025); the non-team market is 0.553 (p = 0.127), indistinguishable from chance

our_assessment.why: The decomposition is arithmetic and solid. The claim that the markets are 'worse than a constant' is a statement about MAE at n = 9 and the Wilcoxon does not reach significance; it is reported as a baseline comparison, not as a test. An alternative reading cannot be excluded at n = 9: traders may have been pricing whether the effect is real rather than what fraction of pipelines would say so (prices correlate +0.78 with the fraction and +0.66, p = 0.054, with the study's own meta-analytic verdict).

relations.why: Same design, unconnected field, same core finding: independent analysts handed one dataset do not converge on a conclusion. Breznau reports 95.2% of variance unexplained; NARPS reports 20% average distance from consensus. Neither cites the other's field.

The scalar out-of-fold result transplants cleanly -- choices predict precision at CV R2 0.507 and the answer at -0.073. But the pairwise test refutes the strong form: choices are coupled to the map at Mantel rho 0.193, and 0.142 net of smoothness. 'Decisions say nothing about what the answer is' must become a comparison of magnitudes with a stated bound.
relations.asymmetric_note: This is a correction to our own record, not to Breznau et al. The CRI number it corrects (R2 = -0.005) is not wrong as computed; it was over-read as an absence when it was a non-detection.

relations.why: Section 6 of NOTES.md reruns the CRI corpus with the pairwise instrument and a power calibration, withdraws an intermediate result of its own, and restates the CRI conclusion as a bound (rho ~ 0.21 needed for 80% power).

Menkveld's split between standard and nonstandard error is the right vocabulary for what is measured here: the team random intercept (sigma = 0.97-1.32 on the logit scale) is a nonstandard error in the conclusion, and NARPS's own tau of 1.13-1.85 across unthresholded maps is one in the estimate, against a sampling standard deviation of at least 1.0.

Mathur et al. argue that CRI's variation is variation in significance rather than in findings. NARPS is the strongest version of that claim -- map correlation carries no detectable information about the binary conclusion on six of seven hypotheses -- and simultaneously its limit, because the maps themselves are coupled to the choices (c6).

That record measured how often a resolving DATA link fails to deliver the resource (37.7%). Here an open-access STATUS DATABASE asserts a free published PDF at a URL that serves a login wall, which is the same failure one level up. Leaves a measurable question: the shell rate among DOIs Unpaywall labels bronze.

Both are structured elicitations of researcher belief scored against an outcome, and both find that the interesting failure is calibration rather than discrimination. Here it is quantified: 74% of the team market's squared error is a single constant offset, and removing it makes the market the best forecaster available.
Section 6 uses the CRI model-level table already stored in that record's data/ directory to run the pairwise instrument on the sociology corpus.

open_questions: The Mantel test is nearly blind to diffuse association (multi-directional injection: rho 0.038 and 14% power where the 1-D injection gives 0.23 and 99%). What is the right omnibus test of 'do choices determine the estimate'? Distance covariance, or a permutation test on a cross-validated multivariate regression of the map onto the choices -- the second needs the 1 GB image deposit.
Does the team trait survive re-thresholding every map identically? c7 shows the LEVEL moves by up to 0.55 under a common rule; the team-level version of that question needs the unthresholded maps.
Does the same over-dispersion appear in #fincap (Menkveld, 164 teams)? It is the only other corpus here with multiple outcomes per team.
Nobody has been told about the c10 transposition. It is in both the preprint and the published Extended Data Table 1, six years on.
What fraction of DOIs Unpaywall labels `bronze` deliver a payload rather than a shell? The maria2026-shell-or-payload instrument runs unchanged.
